links.note: In 1081 the man cannot decide whether she is an அணங்கு, a choice peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு). 918 says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is called an அணங்கு for those without discerning sense. The same word names a spirit that overpowers a man in both books: here it is a lover's wonder, there a warning, and Parimelazhagar glosses it in 918 as a divine woman who takes life through desire.

1081 only asks whether she is an அணங்கு. In 1082, once she returns his look (நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல்), he says it is like an attacking அணங்கு (தாக்கணங்கு) who has also brought an army. The doubt of the first verse becomes a felt assault in the second, and Parimelazhagar reads 1082 as spoken after he has settled that she is human.

In 1081 his heart reels (மாலும் நெஞ்சு) because it cannot place her among goddess, peahen and woman. In 1112 he scolds the same heart for being confused at flowers (மலர்காணின் மையாத்தி நெஞ்சே), as if her eyes were like what many can see. The confusion moves from what she is to what could be compared with her, and by 1112 he treats it as the heart's error.

1082 says her returning look is like an attacking spirit come with an army (தாக்கணங்கு தானைக்கொண் டன்னது): the look only wounds. 1091 finds two looks in her eyes (இருநோக்கு), one that gives the sickness and one that is its medicine (நோய்நோக்கு ... அந்நோய் மருந்து). The next chapter adds the healing side that 1082 leaves out.

In 775 a warrior whose glaring eye (விழித்த கண்) blinks when a spear is thrown counts that as running away. In 1082 the man looks, and her look answering his (நோக்கெதிர் நோக்குதல்) is like an army brought against him. Both treat meeting another's gaze as combat, one on the battlefield and one at first sight in love.

1082 makes her answering glance an armed host (தானை). 1113, listing her beauties, calls her kohl-lined eyes spears (வேலுண்கண்). The eye as weapon is a fixed figure of the man's praise, used first as his alarm and later as a plain item of description.

765 defines an army as the force that can stand together even if Death comes raging at it (கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும்). In 1083 the man says he now knows what is called Death (கூற்று): it has womanly grace and large warring eyes (பேரமர்க் கட்டு). Both set கூற்று in a battle; the Book of Wealth imagines standing against it, and the lover says he has met it in her eyes.

1083: 'I did not know before (பண்டறியேன்) what Death is; now I know'. 1226: the woman did not know (அறிந்ததிலேன்), while her husband had not left, that evening brings sickness. In both a lover says love has taught what was only a word before, the man at first sight and the woman in separation.

326 says Death that eats life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று) does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 1084 says the eyes of this womanly, artless girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them (கண்டார் உயிருண்ணும் தோற்றம்). The lover gives her eyes the standing epithet of Death, which the previous verse (1083) has just named.

279: the arrow is straight but cruel, the lute bent but sweet, so judge by what a thing does (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்). 1084 sets a girl of womanly gentleness (பெண்டகைப் பேதை) against eyes that look as if they eat lives; Parimelazhagar takes அமர்த்தன as 'were at odds' with her nature. Both verses turn on a form that does not match its effect, one as a rule for judging ascetics and one as a lover's surprise.

1084: her eyes have a look that eats the life of those who see them (உயிருண்ணும்). 1221: the woman tells evening it is not evening but a time that eats the life of those once wed (மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும் வேலை). The same phrase marks what kills each lover: for the man her eyes at first sight, for the woman the evening hour in his absence.

1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe, and says it has all three (இம்மூன்றும் உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar comments that it gives pleasure and pain together. 1091 states that plainly as two looks, one the sickness and one its cure. The puzzled question of 1085 is resolved into a doubleness he can name.

In 1085 the doe (பிணை) is one of three things her look might be, beside Death. In 1089 her doe-like artless look (பிணையேர் மடநோக்கு) and her modesty are ornament enough, so added jewels are pointless. The same doe glance is first one part of a threat and then her natural adornment.

1086 wishes her brows would screen her eyes (மறைப்பின்), for then the eyes would not cause him trembling pain. 1087 says the cloth over her breasts is like the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes (கட்படாம்). Both are about a covering over something that harms him: one he wishes for and one he sees, and Parimelazhagar says of the second that the cloth keeps them from killing.

In 1086 the man says her eyes cause him trembling pain (நடுங்கஞர்) and wishes them screened. In 1171 the woman asks why her own eyes weep, since they showed him to her and so gave her this unending sickness (தண்டாநோய் தாம்காட்ட). Each lover names eyes as the cause of the pain; for him it is hers, for her it is her own.

1087: the cloth over her firm breasts is the face-cloth on a rutting bull elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம்). 24: the renouncer guards the five senses with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான்), a goad being the elephant-driver's tool. Both draw on the dangerous elephant held in check; the ascetic chapter makes the senses the elephant, and the lover makes her covered breasts the elephant.

1088: his might (பீடு), feared even by enemies in battle, has broken (உடைந்ததே) before her bright forehead alone. 1258: the woman says the soft words of that deceiving thief are the weapon that breaks her womanly firmness (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). Each lover uses the language of war and breaking for the loss of the quality they prized in themselves, his strength and her restraint.

1088 reports the first loss: his battlefield strength breaks at the sight of her forehead. 1134 says the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). The later verse generalises what 1088 exclaims, with manliness now lost along with shame.

906, in the chapter on being ruled by one's wife, says men who fear her bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no worth even if they live like gods. In 1088 a lover says his might, feared in battle, has broken before her bright forehead. The same pattern, a man's standing undone by a woman's bodily feature, is a censure in the Book of Wealth and a lover's amazed complaint in the Book of Love, where it is his speech and not a ruling.

95: humility and sweet speech are a person's ornament and nothing else is (அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற). 1089: what use are foreign ornaments (ஏதில தந்து அணி) to one who has a doe's artless look and modesty? Both deny that added adornment counts beside an inborn quality, 95 as a rule of conduct and 1089 as a lover's praise.

1014: is not having shame an ornament to the worthy (அணியன்றோ நாணுடைமை)? 1089 counts her modesty (நாண்) with her doe-like look as adornment enough. Both call நாண் an ornament; the nearby 1011 separates the shame of bright-browed women from shame at wrong actions, so the two verses praise different kinds of நாண் with the same figure.

1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe (பிணை). 1089 names the doe-like artless look (பிணையேர் மடநோக்கு) as her natural ornament. The chapter's doe glance appears once beside Death and once as beauty that needs nothing added.

1090: brewed liquor (அடுநறா) delights only those who drink it, not, like love, those who merely see (கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று). 1281: to be elated at a thought and glad at a sight (காண மகிழ்தல்) belongs to love and not to liquor. The same contrast is made twice, at the first meeting and again by the woman late in the book, where thinking is added to seeing.

1090 puts love above liquor because it delights by sight alone. 1201 says love is sweeter than liquor (கள்ளினும் காமம் இனிது) because even thinking of it (உள்ளினும்) gives great joy that does not end. The comparison is extended from the lover who sees to the lover who is apart and only remembers.

1090 uses liquor as the lesser pleasure that love outdoes. 1288 uses it as an exact likeness: 'your chest is to us as liquor is to those who are drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), though it does shaming harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா)'. The later verse grants what 1090 leaves unsaid, that the pull likened to drink goes on despite disgrace.

27 lists the five, taste, light, touch, sound and smell (சுவை ஒளி ஊறு ஓசை நாற்றம்), and says the world lies with the one who discerns their kinds. 1101 lists seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching (கண்டு கேட்டு உண்டு உயிர்த்து உற்று) and says all five are found in this bright-bangled woman alone (ஒண்தொடி கண்ணே உள). The same inventory of the senses is used in the renouncers' chapter for mastery of them and by the lover for their complete enjoyment in one person.

65: touching one's children is joy to the body and hearing their words is joy to the ear. 1101: the objects of all five senses are in her. Both describe a loved person sense by sense; the householder's verse names two senses and children, the lover's names all five and one woman.

1091: her eyes hold two looks, one the sickness and the other its medicine (நோய்நோக்கு ... அந்நோய் மருந்து). 1102: for other diseases the medicine is something else (பிணிக்கு மருந்து பிற), but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). The idea moves from her glance to her person, and from signs before union to union itself.

15: it is rain that ruins, and rain again that stands by the ruined and lifts them up (கெடுப்பதூஉம் ... எடுப்பதூஉம் எல்லாம் மழை). 1102: she is the cure for the sickness she herself gives. Both locate harm and remedy in one source, rain for the world and the beloved for the lover.

948 tells the healer to examine the disease, then its root (நோய்முதல்), then the means that subdue it (அது தணிக்கும் வாய்), as three separate things. 1102 first grants the ordinary rule, that the medicine is other than the disease, and then says love is the exception, where cause and remedy are the same person. The lover's verse marks love's sickness as a case the method of 948 does not cover.

1103: is the world of the lotus-eyed one (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு) sweeter than sleep on the soft shoulders of the one you love? 1323: is there a land of the gods (புத்தேள் நாடு) to compare with sulking with one joined to you like water with earth? Both use the same rhetorical question to set a lover's pleasure above heaven, the first for sleep in her arms and the second for the quarrel.

213 says that in the world of the gods or here (புத்தேளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும்) it is hard to find another good like ஒப்புரவு, doing one's part for others. 1103 asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world is as sweet as sleeping on the beloved's shoulders. Both measure an earthly thing against heaven and prefer it; in the Book of Virtue it is a duty, and here it is a lover's own claim about his pleasure.

1104: the man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). 1159: fire burns only if touched; can it burn when one lets go, as love's sickness does (விடிற்சுடல் ஆற்றுமோ தீ)? The same reversed fire is described from both sides, by the man after union and in the chapter on being unable to bear parting.

691: those who serve quarrelsome kings should be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor coming close (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). 1104: her fire burns at a distance and cools up close. Both reason about fire and distance; the king's fire follows the ordinary rule and calls for a middle distance, while the lover says hers reverses it, so only nearness is safe.

265: austerity is practised here because whatever is wanted is obtained as it is wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால்). 1105: her shoulders are like each desired thing at the moment of desiring it (வேட்ட பொழுதின் அவையவை போலுமே). Both describe desire met exactly as it arises, promised to the ascetic through தவம் and claimed by the lover in her embrace.

1101 says the objects of all five senses are found in her alone. 1105 says her shoulders are like whatever one craves, at the time one craves it. The first claim is about range, that she holds every kind of pleasure; the second adds timing, that she answers each wish as it comes.

78: a life with no love inside is like a dried-up tree putting out shoots on hard ground (வற்றல் மரந்தளிர்த் தற்று), which cannot happen. 1106: each time he reaches her, her touch makes his life put out shoots (உயிர்தளிர்ப்பத் தீண்டலால்), so her shoulders must be made of ambrosia. Both speak of a life sprouting like a plant; without love it cannot, and in the lover's verse it does at every embrace.

1106: his life sprouts afresh whenever he touches her. 1124: she is to his life what living is when they are together, and what dying is when she leaves (வாழ்தல் உயிர்க்கன்னள் ... சாதல் அதற்கன்னள்). Both tie his உயிர் to her presence; 1124 states the other half, which 1106's 'each time' (உறுதோறு) implies.

64: gruel stirred by the small hands of one's own children is far sweeter than ambrosia (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே). 1106: her shoulders are made of ambrosia (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன) because their touch revives his life. Parent and lover both reach for அமிழ்து to measure the nearness of someone of their own; the parent ranks the child's gruel above it and the lover equates her with it.

1065: though it is gruel thin as clear water, nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort gave (தாள்தந்தது உண்ணலின் ஊங்கினியது இல்). 1107 takes that pleasure as its standard: her embrace is like living in one's own house and eating one's own after sharing (தம்மில் இருந்து தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று). The lover's simile assumes what 1065 states, that one's own food is the sweetest.

44: if a household fears blame and shares its food (பாத்தூண்), its line never fails. 1107 uses the same shared meal (பாத்து உண்டு) as the likeness for the joy of embracing her. What the Book of Virtue commends as duty with a reward, the lover treats as a known pleasure; Parimelazhagar reads the verse as his answer to her friend, who urges marriage and the householder's life.

229: eating alone to fill one's own store (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging. 1107: eating one's own after sharing it, in one's own house, is the model of sweetness, and the embrace is like it. Read together they give both halves of one judgement on eating: bitter when hoarded, sweet when shared.

1108: sweet to two who desire each other is an embrace that air cannot cut through (வளியிடை போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு). 1239: when a cool breeze did cut into their embrace (முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழ), her large eyes turned pale. The same words describe the ideal and its smallest breach, and the later verse shows the cost of what 1108 rules out.

1108 praises the embrace with no gap. In 1187 the woman says she lay embracing, shifted a little (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up. The woman's verse gives a reason from her side why the unbroken embrace is the sweet one: the least separation brings the pallor of parting.

1108 specifies 'two who desire' (வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே): the close embrace is sweet to both. 1196: love on one side only is painful, and like a carrying pole it is sweet on both ends (இருதலையானும் இனிது). Both make sweetness depend on the love being mutual, 1108 in fulfilment and 1196 from the woman who lacks it.

1109: sulking, understanding and union (ஊடல் உணர்தல் புணர்தல்) are the gains of those who have come together in love. 1330, the last verse of the book: sulking is love's pleasure, and its pleasure is to join and embrace (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்). The early verse lists the cycle and the closing verse restates it as the nature of love's joy, so the book's final chapters develop what 1109 names in one line.

1109 names quarrel, making up and union together as rewards without ranking them. 1326 ranks them: as digesting is sweeter than eating, sulking is sweeter than union (புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது). The later verse takes one item from 1109's list and gives it first place.

1109 counts sulking (ஊடல்) among the fruits of love. 1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount, and letting it run a little long is like a little too much salt (சிறிது மிக்கற்றால் நீள விடல்). The later verse sets a limit on the first item of 1109's list: it is a gain only in measure.

783: the more one studies a book the more its worth shows (நவில்தொறும் நூல்நயம்), and so it is with the bond of people of character the more one keeps their company (பயில்தொறும்). 1110: as each act of knowing shows one's ignorance (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்று), so is love with each closeness to her (செறிதோறும்). Both use learning, with the same -தொறும் construction, to say that a bond deepens with practice, one for friendship and one for desire.

1145: as drinking is wanted more each time one gets drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்று), love is sweeter each time it is exposed. 1110: love is like finding one's ignorance each time one learns, each time he is close to her. Both say love grows by repetition and does not wear out; 1110 takes its likeness from knowledge and 1145 from drink, and they differ in what is repeated, union or exposure by gossip.

940: as a gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம்), life loves itself more with each suffering (உழத்தொறூஉம்). 1110: each closeness shows love to be more than he knew, as each learning shows ignorance. Both describe an attachment that grows through its own repetition; the gambling chapter gives it as a warning and the lover as a delight.
